title: Working out new words: prefixes and suffixes

tips.title: Peel off one piece
tips.body: Every built word on the papers has exactly one piece added: a prefix like *in-* or a suffix like *-ment*. Peel it off, name the word underneath, then put the meaning back: *in-* is *not*, *-ment* is *-ly*, *-ation* is *the act of*, *-ième* is *-th*.

tips.title: Im- before p, b and m
tips.body: Say *inpossible* and your lips have already closed for the *p*, so French writes the sound it makes: *impossible*, *immobile*. Before *l* and *r* it doubles the consonant instead: *illégal*, *irrégulier*. Before every other letter the prefix is *in-*: *inconnu*, *inutile*, *injuste*.

tips.title: -amment and -emment sound the same
tips.body: *Suffisamment* and *patiemment* end in the same sound. In a dictation, work out the adjective first: *suffisant* has an *a*, *patient* has an *e*, and the adverb keeps that letter.

tips.title: A built word still agrees
tips.body: *La réservation* is feminine, so *une réservation incorrecte*. *Joueur* is masculine, so a woman is *une joueuse*. Building the word does not switch the grammar off.

tips.title: Premier is the only odd ordinal
tips.body: Every ordinal is the number plus *-ième* except *first*, which is *premier* or *première*. Three spellings change on the way: a final *-e* drops (*quatre* → *quatrième*), *cinquième* gains a *u*, and *neuvième* turns *f* into *v*.

why.matters: The Pearson vocabulary list is long, but the Reading paper can also use words made from listed words by a handful of rules the specification sets out. A student who knows *patient* and the rules can read *impatient* and *patiemment* without ever having learnt them. The same rules make dictation easier, because *-amment* and *-emment* sound alike and only the base word tells you which to write. They are a small set of rules that multiply the vocabulary you already have.

examples.title: One step from a word you know
examples.body: From *heureux* (happy), the feminine *heureuse* plus *-ment* gives *heureusement* (fortunately): one piece added. *Malheureusement* (unfortunately) would need two pieces, so the vocabulary list gives it as a word of its own. A built word on the papers is never more than one step from a word you have learnt.

visual.alt: A table showing heureux on the vocabulary list, heureusement built from it with one piece, and malheureusement listed as a word of its own

examples.title: La sixième
examples.body: In a French school, *la sixième* is not just *the sixth*: it is the first year of *collège*, which matches Year 7. The ordinal rule tells you the word, and the context tells you it is a school year. Built words still need the sentence around them.

visual.alt: A table of French school years named with ordinals, the number each is built from, and the English school year it matches

steps.title: Why a word you have never seen can still be one you know
steps.body:
The Pearson vocabulary list is the full set of words the papers use. But the specification also lists a small set of **word-building rules** (spec pages 168–169), and the **Reading** paper may use a word made from a listed word by one of those rules. If you know *possible* and the rule for *im-*, then *impossible* is not a new word. It works backwards too: because *particulièrement* is on the list, the Reading paper may use *particulier*.

Three things the specification promises make this manageable:

- The rules are **few**: one pair of prefixes and four kinds of suffix on both tiers, plus one more at Higher.
- Pearson adds **only one** prefix or suffix to a base word. You will not meet a word with both, such as *impatiemment* built from *patient*.
- Normal grammar endings can still be added on top: *impatientes* is *impatient* plus the feminine plural.

So the method is always the same: **take off the one piece that was added, recognise the word underneath, then put the meaning back together.**

visuals.alt: A table of four known words, the rule applied to each, and the new word it builds

check.solution: *In-* means **not** or **the opposite of**, so *inutile* is *not useful*: **useless**. The prefix never makes a word stronger, and it does not change the word into a verb or an adverb.

steps.title: In- and im-: the opposite
steps.body:
Adding ***in-*** or ***im-*** to an adjective, an adverb or a noun gives its **opposite**, but only where English also uses *un-* or *in-* or means *the opposite of* (spec page 168).

- *possible* → *impossible*
- *patient* → *impatient*
- *connu* (known) → *inconnu* (unknown)
- *juste* (fair) → *injuste* (unfair)
- *sécurité* (safety) → *insécurité* (lack of safety)
- *également* (equally) → *inégalement* (unequally)

***Im-*** is used before **p**, **b** and **m**: *impossible*, *immobile*. Before *l* and *r* it becomes *il-* and *ir-* (*illégal*, *irrégulier*); everywhere else it is ***in-***.

English sometimes uses *un-* where French uses *in-*: *inconnu* is *unknown*, not *inknown*. Read the meaning, not the letters.

French has other negative prefixes too, such as *dé-* in *défaire* and *mé-* in *mécontent*. The specification's rule covers *in-* and *im-* only.

props.title: In- and im- make the opposite

visuals.alt: A table of base words with in- or im- added and the English meaning, showing that English sometimes uses un- instead

check.prompt: You know *connu* (known). What does *inconnu* mean? Give one English word.
check.solution: **Unknown.** *In-* makes the opposite, and English uses *un-* for this word, not *in-*.

steps.title: Suffixes that make nouns and adjectives
steps.body:
Three suffixes on **both tiers** turn one kind of word into another.

**-ième makes an ordinal** (*-th*). Add it to the number, dropping a final *-e*: *six* → *sixième*, *quatre* → *quatrième*, *douze* → *douzième*. Two spelling changes: *cinq* → *cinquième* (a *u* is added) and *neuf* → *neuvième* (*f* becomes *v*). *First* does not follow the rule: it is *premier* or *première*.

**-ation or -ion makes a noun from a verb** (*the act of*), where English has *-ion* or *-ation*. Take the *-er* off and add *-ation*:

- *préparer* → *préparation*
- *réserver* → *réservation*
- *inviter* → *invitation*
- *organiser* → *organisation*
- *inventer* → *invention* (*-ion* straight on the stem)

All of these nouns are **feminine**: *la réservation*.

**-able makes an adjective from a verb**, where English has *-able* or *-ible*: *accepter* → *acceptable*, *recycler* → *recyclable*, *utiliser* → *utilisable* (usable). After a *g*, keep the *e* so the *g* stays soft: *changer* → *changeable*, *manger* → *mangeable*.

props.title: From a verb to a noun or an adjective

visuals.alt: A table of verbs with the nouns made by adding -ation and the adjectives made by adding -able

visuals.fallback: Des mots construits: la cinquième — the fifth; la préparation — preparation; la réservation — booking; recyclable — recyclable; utilisable — usable; heureusement — fortunately; patiemment — patiently; le joueur — player

check.solution: ***La réservation.*** Take *-er* off *réserver* and add *-ation*. Nouns made this way are feminine.

steps.title: Adverbs: -ment, -amment and -emment
steps.body:
English makes most adverbs with *-ly*. French adds ***-ment*** to the **feminine** adjective (spec page 169):

- *heureux* → *heureuse* → *heureusement* (fortunately)
- *sérieux* → *sérieuse* → *sérieusement* (seriously)
- *premier* → *première* → *premièrement* (firstly)
- *seul* → *seule* → *seulement* (only)

When the masculine adjective ends in *-ai*, *-é*, *-i* or *-u*, French adds *-ment* to the masculine: *vrai* → *vraiment*, *poli* → *poliment*, *absolu* → *absolument*. Learn those as they come.

Most adjectives ending in ***-ant*** or ***-ent*** work differently: drop the *-ant* or *-ent* and add ***-amment*** or ***-emment***. Watch *lent* (slow): it takes the ordinary rule, *lente* → *lentement* (slowly).

- *suffisant* → *suffisamment* (enough, sufficiently)
- *patient* → *patiemment*
- *évident* → *évidemment* (obviously)
- *récent* → *récemment*

**Listen out:** *-amment* and *-emment* sound **the same**, like the *a* in *patte* followed by *-ment*. That matters in a dictation: *récemment* has an *e* you cannot hear.

props.title: Two ways to make an adverb

visuals.alt: A table of adjectives, their feminine form where used, and the adverb made with -ment, -amment or -emment

check.solution: ***Patiemment.*** *Patient* ends in *-ent*, so the *-ent* goes and *-emment* is added. *-Ement* on the feminine is the rule for other adjectives, and *-amment* belongs to *-ant* adjectives like *suffisant*.

steps.title: Higher: the person who does it, -eur and -ateur
steps.body:
One suffix is on the **Higher tier** only: ***-eur*** or ***-ateur*** added to a verb stem makes the **person who does it** (spec page 168), like English *-er* or *-or*. *Joueur* and *chanteur* are on the vocabulary list for both tiers already; the rule is for the ones that are not, such as *danseur*, *porteur*, *organisateur* and *présentateur*.

- *jouer* → *joueur* (player)
- *chanter* → *chanteur* (singer)
- *porter* → *porteur* (carrier, porter)
- *organiser* → *organisateur* (organiser)
- *présenter* → *présentateur* (presenter)

The feminine follows the pattern on the grammar list for nouns (spec page 154): ***-eur*** becomes ***-euse***, and ***-teur*** in these *-ateur* words becomes ***-trice***.

- *un joueur* → *une joueuse*
- *un chanteur* → *une chanteuse*
- *un organisateur* → *une organisatrice*
- *un présentateur* → *une présentatrice*

visuals.alt: A table of verbs with the masculine agent noun in -eur or -ateur and the feminine in -euse or -atrice

check.prompt: You know *danser*. What is the word for **a (male) dancer**?
check.solution: ***Un danseur.*** Take *-er* off *danser* and add *-eur*: the person who dances. A female dancer is *une danseuse*.

steps.title: Reading a sentence with two built words
steps.body: In a reading text the built words are usually surrounded by words you know. Take off the piece, find the base, then check the meaning fits the sentence.

visuals.problem: *Malheureusement, la réservation était incorrecte et l'hôtel était complet.*

steps.text: *Malheureusement*: this one is on the vocabulary list as a word of its own, so you know it: **unfortunately**.
*Réservation*: take off *-ation* and put back *-er*: *réserver*, to book. So **the booking**.

*Incorrecte*: take off *in-* and you have *correcte*, the same as English *correct* (it is not on the list itself, so here you lean on English). So **incorrect**, in the feminine to agree with *la réservation*.
Unfortunately, the booking was wrong and the hotel was full.

visuals.problem: *Elle est arrivée cinquième, derrière quatre joueuses professionnelles.*

steps.text: *Joueuses*: *jouer* plus *-eur*, in the feminine plural. So **players**, all women.
steps.note: joueur is a listed word; -euse is its feminine

steps.text: She came fifth, behind four professional players.

check.prompt: What does *la préparation de l'examen était impossible* mean?
check.solution: *Préparation* is the noun from *préparer*, the act of preparing, and *impossible* is *possible* with *im-*. So it was **the preparation** that was impossible. The sentence says nothing about passing, and *im-* makes a word negative, never *very*.

markScheme.description: Preparing for the exam was impossible.

options: Preparing for the exam was impossible.
The exam was not prepared at all.
The exam was impossible to pass.
The exam preparation was very possible.

steps.title: À toi : déconstruire
steps.body:
For each word, write the base word you know and the meaning of the new one. Then check the table.

1. *la sixième*
2. *inégal*
3. *utilisable*
4. *récemment*
5. *une présentatrice*

For 4, remember that *-emment* comes from an *-ent* adjective. For 5, work back from *-trice* to *-teur*, then to the verb.

props.title: Answers

visuals.alt: A table of five built words with the base word each comes from and its meaning

check.prompt: What does *récemment* mean? Give one English word.
check.solution: **Recently.** *Récemment* comes from *récent*, which ends in *-ent*, so the adverb ends in *-emment*.

steps.title: When the rule does not apply
steps.body:
The rules work only where the specification says they do, and a grade 9 reader knows where they stop.

- **English decides.** *In-* is only used where English has *un-*, *in-* or means *the opposite of*, and *-ation* only where English has *-ation* or *-ion*. So the rules help you read; they do not license you to invent words when you write. *Incontent* is not French: *not happy* is *mécontent*.
- **One affix at a time.** Pearson will not add both a prefix and a suffix to one base word in its papers. If a long word seems to have two, it is on the list as a word in its own right: *malheureusement* would be *heureux* plus two pieces, so it is listed itself.
- **False friends survive the rules.** A built word can still mean something unexpected. *Actuellement* is *actuel* + *-ment*, and *actuel* means *current*, so *actuellement* means **currently**, not *actually*.
- **Grammar goes on top.** A built word still agrees: *une réservation incorrecte*, *des joueuses*.

rows: also Year 7 in a French school

visuals.alt: A table of built words that look like one English word but mean another, or carry a grammar ending

check.prompt: What does *actuellement, je travaille dans un café* mean?
check.solution: *Actuellement* is built from *actuel*, which means *current*, so the adverb means **currently** or **at the moment**. It is a false friend of *actually*. *Used to* would need the imperfect, and nothing in the sentence is negative.

At the moment, I work in a café.
In fact, I no longer work in a café.
Actually, I work in a café.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- *In-* / *im-* (before p, b, m) make the opposite: *impossible*, *inconnu*.
- *-ième* makes ordinals: *cinquième*, *neuvième*; but *premier*.
- *-ation* makes a feminine noun from a verb: *la réservation*.
- *-able* makes an adjective from a verb: *recyclable*, *changeable*.
- *-ment* on the feminine adjective makes an adverb; *-ant* and *-ent* give *-amment* and *-emment*, which sound alike.
- Higher: *-eur* / *-ateur* make the person who does it; feminine *-euse* / *-atrice*.
- Pearson adds only one affix per word, and the rules help you read rather than invent.

visuals.alt: A summary table of which word-building rules are on both tiers and which is Higher only

questions.solution: *In-* makes **the opposite**, so *injuste* is **unfair**. The prefix does not make a word stronger or turn it into a noun.
***La cinquième.*** *Cinq* + *-ième*, with a *u* added so the *q* is followed by *u* as usual in French.
*Heureusement* is *heureuse* + *-ment*, the *-ly* ending, so it is an adverb: **fortunately**. *Happiness* would be a noun (*le bonheur*), and *unfortunately* would be *malheureusement*.

questions.prompt: You know *possible*. Write the French word for **impossible**.
questions.solution: ***Impossible.*** *Im-* rather than *in-*, because the base word starts with *p*.
***L'invitation.*** Take *-er* off *inviter* and add *-ation*. It is feminine, like every noun made this way.
***Sérieusement.*** *-Ment* goes on the feminine *sérieuse*, not on the masculine *sérieux*. *-Emment* is only for adjectives ending in *-ent*, such as *patient* and *récent*.

questions.prompt: What does *recyclable* mean? Give one English word.
questions.solution: **Recyclable.** *Recycler* + *-able*: it can be recycled. English uses the same word.
***Neuvième.*** *Neuf* + *-ième*, with the *f* changing to *v* between vowels. The ending is always *-ième*.

questions.prompt: What does *évidemment* mean? Give one English word.
questions.solution: **Obviously.** *Évident* ends in *-ent*, so the adverb drops *-ent* and adds *-emment*. *Evidently* is right too.

questions.prompt: What does *cette application est utilisable sans connexion* mean?
questions.solution: *Utilisable* is *utiliser* + *-able*: it **can be used**. *Useful* is a different word, *utile*, and *useless* would be *inutile*. *-Able* makes an adjective, not a past tense, so *was used* does not fit.

markScheme.description: This app can be used without a connection.

options: This app is useful without a connection.
This app can be used without a connection.
This app was used without a connection.
This app is useless without a connection.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a word that is not French?
questions.solution: *Incontent* is not French: *not happy* is *mécontent*. The prefix rule only applies where English has *un-*, *in-* or means *the opposite*, and it helps you read words that exist rather than build new ones. *Impossible*, *inutile* and *incorrect* are all real words.

questions.prompt: You know *présenter*. Write the French for **a female presenter**.
questions.solution: ***Une présentatrice.*** *Présenter* gives *présentateur*, and *-teur* becomes *-trice* in the feminine.

questions.prompt: What does *elle a répondu patiemment au patient* mean?
questions.solution: *Patiemment* is *patient* with *-emment*, the *-ly* ending, so she answered **patiently**. *Au patient* is the noun, the person in hospital. *Impatiently* would need *im-*, and *elle* is the one who answered.
options: She was a patient who answered.

questions.solution: ***Récemment.*** *Récent* ends in *-ent*, so drop it and add *-emment*. It sounds like *récamment*, so the spelling comes from the adjective.
*Actuellement* is *actuel* (current) + *-ment*, so it means **currently**. It is a false friend of *actually*, which is *en fait*.

questions.prompt: Pearson applies at most one prefix or suffix to a base word. You meet *malheureusement* (unfortunately), which looks like *mal-* + *heureux* + *-ment*. What follows?
questions.solution: Because Pearson never adds two pieces, *malheureusement* cannot be *heureux* with two additions, so it must be **on the vocabulary list itself**, and it is. It can appear on any paper, and *mal-* reverses the meaning: *unfortunately*, not *happily*.

markScheme.description: It is a word to learn in its own right, since two additions are never made.

options: It is built from heureux by two additions, so it can be worked out.
It is a word to learn in its own right, since two additions are never made.
It cannot appear on a Reading paper at all.
It must mean happily, because heureux means happy.

questions.prompt:
Read the text and answer in English.

*Récemment, notre collège a organisé un concours de musique. Malheureusement, la préparation était difficile, parce que les organisatrices étaient toujours occupées. Ma sœur est arrivée cinquième. Elle a attendu patiemment son tour et elle était calme, mais pour moi, le résultat était injuste.*

1. When did the competition take place?
2. Why was the preparation difficult?
3. What place did the sister come?
4. How did she wait for her turn?
5. What does the writer think of the result?
6. Give two words in the text built by adding a suffix to a word you know, and say what each means.
questions.solution:
**Model answer.**

1. Recently.
2. The organisers (women) were always busy.
3. Fifth.
4. Patiently (and she was calm).
5. It was unfair.
6. Any two of: *récemment* (recently, from *récent*), *préparation* (preparation, from *préparer*), *organisatrices* (organisers, from *organiser*, Higher), *cinquième* (fifth, from *cinq*), *patiemment* (patiently, from *patient*).

**What earns the marks.** Every answer is in English, as the Reading paper requires. Each built word is read by taking off one piece: *-emment* and *-ment* are *-ly*, *-ation* is the act of, *-trice* is the woman who does it, and *-ième* is *-th*. *Injuste* is *juste* with *in-*, so it means unfair.

questions.prompt:
Translate into English:

*Actuellement, je travaille comme serveur dans un restaurant. Heureusement, mon patron est patient, mais les clients sont souvent impatients. La réservation de ce soir est impossible à trouver, et la cinquième table attend depuis vingt minutes.*
questions.solution:
**Model answer.**

At the moment, I work as a waiter in a restaurant. Fortunately, my boss is patient, but the customers are often impatient. Tonight's booking is impossible to find, and the fifth table has been waiting for twenty minutes.

**What earns the marks.** *Actuellement* is *currently*, never *actually*. *Heureusement* is *heureuse* + *-ment*, and *impatients* is *patient* with *im-* and a plural ending. *Réservation* is the noun from *réserver*, and *cinquième* is *cinq* + *-ième*. *Attend depuis vingt minutes* is the present with *depuis*, so English needs *has been waiting*, not *waits since*.

markScheme.description: booking, impossible, fifth table, has been waiting

criteria.text: First sentence: currently or at the moment, not actually
Second sentence: fortunately, patient, impatient, with the contrast kept
Third sentence: booking, impossible, fifth table, has been waiting for twenty minutes

examTechnique.body:
In **reading**, when a word looks new, try the rules before you guess: take off *in-* or *im-*, *-ment*, *-amment* or *-emment*, *-ation*, *-able*, *-ième* or, at Higher, *-eur* and *-ateur*, and see whether you know what is left. Pearson adds only one piece to a base word, and grammar endings may sit on top.

In **translation into English**, turn the built word into natural English: *-ment* is usually *-ly*, *-ation* is often *-ation*, *in-* can be *un-*. Watch false friends: *actuellement* is *currently*.

In **dictation**, spell an adverb from the adjective you know: *-amment* after *-ant*, *-emment* after *-ent*. In **writing**, use built words you have met; the rules are for reading, not for inventing.
examinerErrors: Writing *-amment* where the adjective ends in *-ent*: *patiamment*.
Reading *in-* as making a word stronger rather than opposite.
Forgetting the feminine agreement on a built word: *la réservation incorrect*.
Inventing a word with a prefix that French does not use: *incontent*.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 reader meets an unfamiliar word calmly: it strips one prefix or suffix, recognises the listed word underneath, and checks that the meaning fits the sentence. It knows where the rules stop, reads *actuellement* as *currently*, spells *-amment* and *-emment* from the adjective in a dictation, and makes a built word agree. In translation it turns each built word into natural English rather than a letter-by-letter copy.
